extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, historians of mathematics, and mathematicians interested in diagram-based Euclidean reasoning and its justificatory practice
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and principles for constructing and assessing Euclidean-style diagram-based proofs in plane geometry, including how diagrams may license inferences, how generality is secured, and how sensitive or exceptional cases must be handled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstration step structure and diagram responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstration steps are discrete sequences of claims, each licensed by prior claims and the 'current' diagram; beyond text–text licensing, steps may draw from the diagram (diagram-based premises) and may take responsibility for additional diagram elements (diagram-based conclusions). The current diagram consists only of items previously so introduced together with regions, segments, and distinguished points arising by their interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text records when a diagram element is admitted (e.g. 'let AB be the given straight segment' does not yet admit a circle centered at A). Track how far 'taking responsibility' for parts of the diagram has progressed via the linear structure of the proof. The general form of a single demonstration-step license: claims in prior text, attributions to current diagram → new claims in text, new elements in diagram. Not all entries need be present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagram-based attribution: exact vs co-exact
rubrics_metrics.description: Only certain kinds of claims may be licensed on the basis of diagram appearance: co-exact claims (conditions insensitive to a range of variation in diagram entries) may be attributed from the diagram; exact claims (equalities of non-identicals, proportionalities, etc.) must not be claimed on the basis of appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Co-exact conditions include part–whole relations of regions, segments bounding regions, and lower-dimensional counterparts; these form the diagram's 'appearance'. Exact metric conditions (equalities, proportions) are never claimed from mere appearance. Many naive criticisms of diagram use mistakenly assume exact claims are read off diagrams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements and recording for diagram entries
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagram entries in elementary geometry are (typically) line segments and circles (Postulates I.1–3, directly or via constructions). Whenever an entry is made, the text records its exact character (e.g. straight, circular).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entries must be adequate with respect to both co-exact and exact character: at minimum continuous non–self-intersecting curves, a line segment connecting its endpoints, a circle closed. Participants can apply co-exact criteria decisively (diagram size permitting). Egregiously non-straight or non-circular entries can be immediately rejected; some inexactness may require deferred rejection via challenges to later attributions. Note that one-dimensional entries control zero- and two-dimensional entries (points, regions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-branching when constructions yield different appearances
rubrics_metrics.description: Because additional entries may change the diagram's attributable co-exact character depending on metric features, demonstrations must allow for case-branching: separate diagram and continuation where different attributions arise from instances of the initial configuration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two families of strategies to determine relevant cases: (a) enumeration/exclusion (explicitly enumerate conceivable topological arrangements and argue to exclude unrealizable ones — Miller), and (b) diagram control (use constructions and physical diagram production to limit possible appearances — Manders). Limiting case-branching to only when a different-appearance feature is actually attributed (Mumma) reduces the number of cases to those found in Euclid. Case-branching must be exhaustive for generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity avoidance and diagram clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Some co-exact attributions may be 'sensitive' to small changes or to drawing inaccuracies; demonstrations must avoid sensitive diagram situations or supply means to make attributions secure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two principal mechanisms: (a) keep diagrams simple by breaking developments into separate propositions (avoid carrying construction lines unnecessarily), and (b) require diagrams to be large/clear enough to support attributions (avoid 'smudges'); where an exact condition is to be shown failing, use an exaggerated drawing. If a diagram does not provide a clear case for a co-exact attribution, the attribution should be rejected or the diagram re-drawn. Sensitivity-avoidance and possible deferred rejection are part of justificatory practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope via setting-out statements and non-triviality
rubrics_metrics.description: A demonstration's range of generality is conceptualized in advance by its setting-out statement (ekthesis) — e.g. 'let AB be the given finite straight line' — which specifies the UG (universal generalization) scope and excludes trivial/singular instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional demonstrations claim to establish propositions only for non-trivial instances (those where items like angles and triangles contain proper regions); singular limiting cases are treated separately or regarded as exceptions. The setting-out statement makes explicit the domain of instances for which diagram-based attributions must be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of reasoning: prohibit reliance on incidental diagram features
rubrics_metrics.description: Because drawn diagrams display many distinctive features, Euclidean uniformity of reasoning is secured not by representational 'placeholders' but by prohibiting differential responses to incidental features: licence diagram-based attributions only for co-exact conditions clearly displayed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern logical/general-algebraic methods achieve uniformity via representation-enforced unresponsiveness (letters/placeholders). Euclid achieves effective uniformity by limiting diagram-based inferences to stable (co-exact) features; proofs must avoid relying on irrelevant right angles, equalities, or other incidental features of a particular diagram unless those features are explicitly within the demonstration's scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite case structure and methods for locating relevant cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Although diagrams may hide many potential cases, the topology of ideal diagrams (via Tarski/real-closed-field connections) gives finite cell decompositions: the number of relevant cases for a claim is finite and their boundaries can be systematically explored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mathematical-topological perspective implies that keeping diagrams simple helps control case complexity and that case boundaries may be found by exploring definable-set boundaries. Mumma's ongoing work applies this to expand analysis of case distinctions in Euclidean geometry; practitioners may use such methods to justify that all cases have been covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to special case (valid strategy when accompanied by reduction argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduction to a specially chosen case (one with advantageous special features) can justify a general claim provided there is a separate reduction argument showing that any instance of the general hypothesis may be connected to the special configuration (e.g. via projections, invariants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This strategy differs from relying on generic diagrams: the special-case argument explicitly uses special features and then supplements them by demonstrating projective/invariant connections to the general instances (Poncelet example). Reduction is permissible but must include the reduction step that links the special case back to the general claim.
